Fill in the blanks in the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/b1b5a17a8facd73638545861a9ec05ee2fdebdc2ae8f327fc86f1517085bcd77.png) where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/52808e8499c76638f512feb7dd3721814844cbfb29deb7126ed9e8872a699031.png)*

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\,\,\, \\ 3{e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} \\ \,\,\,\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$
e-21722.worked_solution:
Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $\mathbf x(t_0)$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/ed2abaaded6d82b6ab9ae856b8f31f99d97bd34515715e36b71d2731049e5e75.png) So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-1)} & (t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3(t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/56f10da4c0759fd5616557c00ce5aa1062190b3fbaaa2ab0dff0d50ef3fb2615.png)
So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{4(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{4(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{4s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3(t-1){e}^{4(t-1)} \\ 3{e}^{4(t-1)}\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{4t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

e-21720.knowledge_point: Solving an Inhomogeneous System Using a Given Matrix Exponential
e-21720.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/cf38da5e2aec9fc3957f52abc58fc396686db632561953991a3ca0fc23799ace.png)
Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/1a1e4510a1ea4961976e22504d6be845edffd972cc88dda0fde4608b50be2b09.png) where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/cfc60391cfb7369d109e7d56b89b6bfd1f97e7251aacb637f61c94d24cdb4f00.png)*
e-21720.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/802292289f84a7d69cfaadd91d88d6a4af9560f618dfae6b553fbca16b63cb96.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/a851d7868235cdaf8cd6914d21b648b3bd7453549748f4bacc3caf5485c17e50.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/696a10263a0fe8a52e0da4a413956bb4040220de2c22ae41f76032f7045a5265.png) So, the matrix of the system is ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/c62e0b111e20b925570d7f178ac556293597b071d9aefb821adc70d83afcb91e.png)

Given the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \underbrace{e^{A(t-t_0)} \, \mathbf{x}(t_0)}_{\text{homogeneous part}} + \underbrace{\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)} \mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $\mathbf x(t_0)$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/b7b3cf84162533f6b86e3faf8bba17b335ade35acb42d18aa768a5a1db900730.png)
Since the initial conditions are given at $t = t_0 = 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x(0) & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/5f80485e8a40e46b5c11656dae755f51f7b0617cbe8b4369cf330f329d042283.png)
So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} & (t-s){e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0 & {e}^{3(t-s)}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3(t-s)} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3s+3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3s+3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3s+3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/dbce2a7dd9077db8a6e4f85a0b54c9d2563cad3a0ef5a0a98606ca7a4bb5f81f.png)

e-21721.knowledge_point: Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution of an Inhomogeneous System
e-21721.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ passing through $\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ is presented below.

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t)$  

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{y}'(t) = -Ae^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t) + e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}'(t)$  

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{y}'(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(t)$  

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{y}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t_0) = \int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{y}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)$ 

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{-A(s-t_0)}\mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s$  

$\textrm{L7}{:}\;$ $\displaystyle e^{A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{y}(t)=e^{A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)}\mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s$

$\textrm{L8}{:}\;$ $e^{A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{y}(t)=\mathbf{x}(t)$

$\textrm{L9}{:}\;$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}(t)=e^{A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t} e^{A(t-s)}\mathbf{g}(s) \, \text{d}s$

Fill in the blanks with the correct reasons to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L3}$ follows from $\textrm{L2}$ by  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/befe715ac2d9375061b1a3c8c0528a0bfb2764197cee4eca4d2b60146cec20b6.png).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L5}$ follows from line $\textrm{L1}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/09febb48bb00d22caebf088103181b5db6377befccad18f1370718351cc91e9d.png).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L8}$ follows from line $\textrm{L1}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/999db06dcfe0878ddb3316b11546668ba9442d8fd110165e5076b90964b84905.png).
e-21721.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\textrm{L2}$ and $\textrm{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
\mathbf{y}'(t) = -Ae^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t) + e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}'(t)
$$

in $\textrm{L2}$ and substituting $\mathbf{x}'(t)=A\mathbf{x}(t)+\mathbf{g}(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\textrm{L3}$ follows from $\textrm{L2}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/9dcfd90e4444195ee781ab388b36a575ec1219d1820f7141114e29311941ddc5.png)

- Next, we consider lines $\textrm{L1}$ and $\textrm{L5}.$ Evaluating $\mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t)$ at $t=t_0$ gives

$$
\mathbf{y}(t_0)=e^{-A(t_0-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t_0)=I\mathbf{x}(t_0)=\mathbf{x}(t_0).
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L5}$ follows from line $\textrm{L1}$  by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/90a07cffb30b2ef860b0d3314865a7bd9ca0b7c86811a63b07628c768188af3e.png)

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L1}$ and $\textrm{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
\mathbf{y}(t)=e^{-A(t-t_0)}\mathbf{x}(t)
$$

from $\textrm{L1}$ by $e^{A(t-t_0)}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L8}$ follows from $\textrm{L1}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14071250/assets/23a2ac9e75c9bac22187814f524d919166d3748f1caa5831d664231a80bac296.png)

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]x+[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,x(1)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

| $x(t)=\,\,$ |  | $3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))$ |  | $\,\,+{\int }_{1}^{t}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  | $\,\,\text{d}s$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-2}} |  |  | ${e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))$ |  |  |  |  |
after.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ {e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ {e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Write down the expression that gives the solution of the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

content.worked_solution:
Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ {e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1)) \\ 3\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-1))\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ {e}^{2s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)+3,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

| $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)$ |  |  |
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+3 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-2x(t)+1,\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

| $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ |  |  |
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(t-s)) \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2(t-s))\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

content.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=y(t)+1 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=x(t),\end{aligned}\,[\begin{aligned}x(0) \\ y(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the solution to the initial value problem above.

*Hint: ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)\end{aligned}],$ where $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$*

| $[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | $\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)-1$ |  |  |
content.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]x(t)+g(t),
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $g(t)=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ So, the matrix of the system is $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

Given the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix, the solution of the initial value problem can be written as the sum of the homogeneous part and a particular solution:

$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that 

$$
{e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Since the initial conditions are given at $t={t}_{0}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})} & ={e}^{At}\,x(0) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]\text{d}s \\  & ={[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sinh}⁡(t-s) \\ -\operatorname{cosh}⁡(t-s)\end{aligned}]}_{s=0}^{s=t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(t) \\ \operatorname{cosh}⁡(t)-1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

after.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by substituting

{{field-4}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$

content.knowledge_point: Proving the Matrix Exponential Formula for IVP Solution of an Inhomogeneous System
content.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by substituting 
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L9}$ follows from line $\text{L7}$ by  
{{field-4}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L6}.$ From $\text{L4}$ we have

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Using $y(0)=x(0)$ from $\text{L5}$, this becomes

$$
y(t)-x(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s,
$$

so

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substituting $y(0)=x(0).$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L7}$ and $\text{L9}.$ From $\text{L8}$ we know that

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).
$$

Substituting ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$ into

$$
{e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s
$$

from $\text{L7}$ gives

$$
x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Therefore, $\text{L9}$ follows from $\text{L7}$ by $\text{substituting }{e}^{At}y(t)=x(t).$

decision.explanation: Substituting x′=Ax+g into L2 cancels the Ax terms, giving L3. Multiplying L6 by e^{At} gives L7 because e^{At}e^{-As}=e^{A(t-s)}. Multiplying L1 by e^{At} gives L8 because e^{At}e^{-At}=I.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by  
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-4}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-At}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

content.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-At}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}{e}^{-At}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

Question 13
?
Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t)

L4: y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L5: y(t0)=x(t0)

L6: y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L7: eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L3 follows from L2 by
 
evaluating at t=t0
applying a change of variables
substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)
substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)+t0
.

Line L5 follows from line L1 by
 
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
differentiating and using the sum rule
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
 
evaluating at t=t0
integrating both sides
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
.
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting x′=Ax+g into L2 cancels the terms containing Ax, yielding L3. Evaluating L1 at t=t₀ gives y(t₀)=e⁰x(t₀)=x(t₀), yielding L5. Multiplying L6 by e^{A(t-t₀)} yields L7 because e^{A(t-t₀)}e^{-A(s-t₀)}=e^{A(t-s)}.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by  
{{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ at $t={t}_{0}$ gives

$$
y({t}_{0})={e}^{-A({t}_{0}-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})=Ix({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$

after.html:
Question 13
?
Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t)

L4: y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L5: y(t0)=x(t0)

L6: y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L7: eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L3 follows from L2 by
evaluating at t=t0
evaluating at t=t0
applying a change of variables
substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)
substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)+t0
.

Line L5 follows from line L1 by
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
differentiating and using the sum rule
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
evaluating at t=t0
integrating both sides
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L2 and L3. Starting from y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t) in L2 and substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t) from the original system gives
    y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)(Ax(t)+g(t))=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)g(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t). Thus, L3 follows from L2 by substituting x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).

  • Next, we consider lines L1 and L5. Evaluating y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t) at t=t0 gives
    y(t0)=e−A(t0−t0)x(t0)=Ix(t0)=x(t0). Therefore, L5 follows from L1 by evaluating at t=t0.

  • Finally, we consider lines L6 and L7. Multiplying both sides of y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds from L6 by eA(t−t0) gives
    eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+eA(t−t0)∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds. Therefore, L7 follows from L6 by multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms all three answers: substituting x′=Ax+g into L2 cancels the Ax terms; evaluating L1 at t=t₀ gives y(t₀)=x(t₀); multiplying L6 by e^{A(t-t₀)} gives L7 using e^{A(t-t₀)}e^{-A(s-t₀)}=e^{A(t-s)}. content.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by  
{{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Starting from

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)
$$

in $\text{L2}$ and substituting ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t)$ from the original system gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}(Ax(t)+g(t)) \\  & =-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t) \\  & ={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{substituting }{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ at $t={t}_{0}$ gives

$$
y({t}_{0})={e}^{-A({t}_{0}-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})=Ix({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$

decision.explanation: Differentiating L1 with the product rule gives L2 since (e^{-At})′=−Ae^{-At}. Integrating L3 from 0 to t gives L4 by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Multiplying L6 by e^{At} gives L7 using e^{At}e^{-As}=e^{A(t-s)}.

after.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line
{{field-2}}
by integrating both sides from $0$ to 
{{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by  
{{field-4}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ from $0$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

content.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x(0)$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y(0)=x(0)$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{At}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by

{{field-2}}

{{field-4}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Differentiating $y(t)={e}^{-At}x(t)$ and applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =({e}^{-At})^{′}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =(-A){e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t) \\  & =-A{e}^{-At}x(t)+{e}^{-At}{x}^{′}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating and using the product rule}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-At}g(t)$ from $0$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y(0)={\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

So, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by integrating both sides from $0$ to $t.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)=x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,ds
$$

from $\text{L6}$ by ${e}^{At}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At}y(t) & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{e}^{At}{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{-As}g(s)\,\text{d}s \\  & ={e}^{At}x(0)+{\int }_{0}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{At}.$

before.html:
Question 15
?
Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t)

L4: y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L5: y(t0)=x(t0)

L6: y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L7: eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L4 follows from L3 by
 
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
evaluating at t=t0
applying a change of variables
integrating both sides from t0 to t
.

Line L5 follows from line L1 by
 
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
differentiating and using the sum rule
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
evaluating at t=t0
.

Line L8 follows from line L1 by
 
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
differentiating and using the sum rule
evaluating at t=t0
.
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating L3 from t₀ to t gives L4 by the fundamental theorem of calculus. Evaluating L1 at t=t₀ gives y(t₀)=Ix(t₀)=x(t₀), yielding L5. Multiplying L1 by e^{A(t-t₀)} cancels e^{-A(t-t₀)}, yielding L8.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-3}}.
after.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$ from ${t}_{0}$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by $\text{integrating both sides from }{t}_{0}\text{ to }t.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ at $t={t}_{0}$ gives

$$
y({t}_{0})={e}^{-A({t}_{0}-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})=Ix({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$

Question 15

Consider the inhomogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t)+g(t), where A is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution x(t) passing through x(t0) is presented below.

L1: Let y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t)

L2: y′(t)=−Ae−A(t−t0)x(t)+e−A(t−t0)x′(t)

L3: y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t)

L4: y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L5: y(t0)=x(t0)

L6: y(t)=x(t0)+∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds

L7: eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

L8: eA(t−t0)y(t)=x(t)

L9: x(t)=eA(t−t0)x(t0)+∫t0teA(t−s)g(s)ds

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

Line L4 follows from L3 by
integrating both sides from t0 to t
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
evaluating at t=t0
applying a change of variables
integrating both sides from t0 to t
.

Line L5 follows from line L1 by
evaluating at t=t0
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
differentiating and using the sum rule
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
evaluating at t=t0
.

Line L8 follows from line L1 by
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
multiplying both sides by eA(t+t0)
multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0)
differentiating and using the sum rule
evaluating at t=t0
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's justify each of the selected steps.

  • We first consider lines L3 and L4. Integrating y′(t)=e−A(t−t0)g(t) from t0 to t in L3 yields
    y(t)−y(t0)=∫t0te−A(s−t0)g(s)ds.
    Thus, L4 follows from L3 by integrating both sides from t0 to t.

  • Next, we consider lines L1 and L5. Evaluating y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t) at t=t0 gives
    y(t0)=e−A(t0−t0)x(t0)=Ix(t0)=x(t0). Therefore, L5 follows from L1 by evaluating at t=t0.

  • Finally, we consider lines L1 and L8. Multiplying both sides of y(t)=e−A(t−t0)x(t) from L1 by eA(t−t0) gives
    eA(t−t0)y(t)=eA(t−t0)e−A(t−t0)x(t)=x(t). Therefore, L8 follows from L1 by multiplying both sides by eA(t−t0).

content.problem:
Consider the inhomogeneous system  ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+g(t),$ where $A$ is a constant square matrix. A derivation of the formula for the solution $x(t)$ passing through $x({t}_{0})$ is presented below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$  

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)=-A{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)+{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}{x}^{′}(t)$  

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$  

$\text{L4}:\,$ $y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $y({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0})$ 

$\text{L6}:\,$ $y(t)=x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s$  

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t)=x(t)$

$\text{L9}:\,$ $x(t)={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})+{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s$

Select the correct options to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by  
{{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by  
{{field-3}}.
content.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Integrating ${y}^{′}(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}g(t)$ from ${t}_{0}$ to $t$ in $\text{L3}$ yields

$$
y(t)-y({t}_{0})={\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{-A(s-{t}_{0})}g(s)\,\text{d}s.
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by $\text{integrating both sides from }{t}_{0}\text{ to }t.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L5}.$ Evaluating $y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)$ at $t={t}_{0}$ gives

$$
y({t}_{0})={e}^{-A({t}_{0}-{t}_{0})}x({t}_{0})=Ix({t}_{0})=x({t}_{0}).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{evaluating at }t={t}_{0}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L8}.$ Multiplying both sides of

$$
y(t)={e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t)
$$

from $\text{L1}$ by ${e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}y(t) & ={e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}{e}^{-A(t-{t}_{0})}x(t) \\  & =x(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{multiplying both sides by }{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}.$
